The first excursion for this season of the Was. rington Field Club was held on siatunlay, when, the day being exceedingly tine, about a score of the ,• members proceeded by the 2.38 train from Arpley tsr Dunham, where they were met by the Rev. G. E. Warburton, vicar of Warburton, who had kindly ! undertaken to conduct the party in their explom- tion of the district. After tea the members pro- ceeded, under the guidance of Mr. Warburton, to I visit the old church, the interior of which was inspected and the more interesting and striking feat ores pointed out. The party then made their way to Watley Station, returniug by the 7.57 train.

div.p: ; Mr.GLAIMITONt's speeches or writings. What would Mr. tacit think if, is face of his speeches, we were to give it an our opinion that he bitterly regrets having opplsed Home Rule ? Let the member. for Newton do as lie would be done by, and not insinuate hypocrisy on the part of a statesman whose boots he is not worthy to black. Auto the Liberal party havMg got Mr. PARNELL's saddle on their back, all we nc,l say is that they are neither driven nor 1.1 by the Irish leader; and, further, that the pace is easy, since he himself is perfectly willing to trust Mr. GLAIKKTONE to help Irdalld in the future as he has helped her in the past. But Tories of the Lacti type see no need of doing anything for Ireland except providing batons, bayonets, and battering-rams. It is the sortie to-day as it was in Dean Swim's time ; the landlonls are permitted to—

Steal by night and steal by day. Doing it all in a legal way, • while the peasantry are left to starve. Dean Swirr,-dignitary though he was of the English Church—told English statesmen the plain truth , when he said that not one Irish tenant out of a hundnid could afford shoes or stockings to his children, or eat flesh, or drink anything better than sour milk and water twice in a year no that the whole country, except the Scotch plantation in tho North, is a scene of misery mid desolation hardly to lie niatched on this side of Lapland." " Oppression," he adds, makes a wise man mad: hut when the Irish show sonie signs of madness, as the inevitable outcome of oppressi, in, Mr. Loon has nothing for them hut misrepresentation, and petty sneers. Ilis progress is backward ;he is not prepared to grant evens" a modified form of self- g,overnmeut." "It was ridiculous," he said, "tin talk of such a thing, and no 111. in his senses , would think of it:' That is to say all the talk we I have heard from the Tory party of treating Ireland as we trout England has been no much nonsense— so much alaior humbug ! Does the member for I Newton not know that Lord RANDOLPH eirreCUILL, Awaking ON the mouthpiece of th Government, promised Ireland local self-govern- moult? Does he not know that a similar promise 1 has sauce noon smile by Lord SALISIIVitt ? And is it " ritlicti/ons to talk of Bach a thing As Mr. Loon thinks fit to raise such an issue, we venture I to say that it seems to us that no one in their senses" could utter such inconsistent jargon as was spouted at the Golborne Conservative Club PI What is the matter with hint to he about to constitute himself a Fifth Party—a party of one Or is he qualifying for Riainnlaill?

Th, THERE was a lively debate in the Exhibition House of Commons, in Tuesday, Blunder' when Mr. E. ROBERTSON moved to reduce the safety of the Foreign Secretary by erloo by way of protest against the manner in which the British Government have boycotted the French Exhibition. Sir JAMES FEBOUSSON, as Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, made a poor defence of the position of the Government. Lord Lrrrox, the British Ambassador at l'aris, applied, he said, for leave of absence in order that he might undergo moffitml treatment ; "list, it would in any ease have been difficult for him to be present and taking part in an event in celebration of a matter ' which was one of internal controversy : and there- fore it was desirable that ho should not be present." Mr. GLADSTONE followed, and made ! short work of this contention. He refemsl to the min:Melon made by Sir JAMES that Lord BEACONS- rieLv had ordered our participation in the cele- bration of the centenary of the American Rowan- Lion, and asked if nobody objected to the Americas Revolution F Mr. Gtsnaroxe added :

There were in America loyalists to the British Crown far mere numerous and ten times more re- spectable than the pnvileged classes in France- ! (Opposition cheers) than the French royalists who ran away from France. The American loyalists in- eluded men who cultb very considerable amount of legal and Conn notional argument which they ad- vanced in favour of the course which they wished to see taken. If we were to be no tender of the feelings of those gentlemen who object to the French Revolution, we might to have had ten times more tender feeling for our brethren of the same blood and language in America. (Opposition cheers).

„ The Government had no answer to this argument, for there in no answer. In matters of this kind, Lord Itascossrmo showed good sense, and if he had been at the head of the Government to-day he would have required Imr Ainbaesador to take part in the ..pa-fling ceremony of the Exhibition or have been present himself. Lord SALMI-11Y has otherwise exercised his discretion, and has not shown himself discreet. He cannot forget that the French Revolution was an outburst of Liberalism ! which was successful, and it gratifies his Toryism 'to boycott its celebration. It is sheer stmoidity to suggest that there is any internal controversy to-day as to the Revolution. It is as much an aocepted fact on the part of the French as is the Revolution of :HIM on the part of the English. • But if sir 'Ga.:mama have made an exhibition of their folly, the people are showing themselves ! wise: they are going in thousands to the Con- ! tennis! Exhibition.

div.head: NEW LORD LIEUTENANT OF IRELAND. .
div.p: THE NEW LORD LIEUTENANT OF IRELAND. .

It is facially announced that the Carl of Zotiand has accepted the po,t of Lord Lieutenant of In.land. His Lordship, who 10 45 yearsof age. was educated at [farrow ' and at Trinity College, C.amlnide',e, and was formerly lieutenaw of the Royal Horse Guards Blue. He sat no member for Richmond (Yorkshire) as a Liberal in 1872-3, in which latter year he aneceeded to the title. He wm Lord-in-Waiting to the Queen in 1880. He was married in 1871 to daughter of the ninth Karl of 8474rty/rough, and 14iIS wveral children.

A deputation of Irish peers and members of Parlia- ment waited upon Lord Salisbury at his how, in Arling- ton-Ste on Wednesday morning.in regard to the lanition of the Irish Viceroyalty. Th,• deputation was intealueed by Lord Waterton). Lord Salisbury said that before he likened to the Vielea of the deputation he thought it wax only fair to state that Lord Zetland had already accepted the offer of the Lord Lieutenancy of Ireland in succession to Lord Londonderry. A memorial was then presented to the Premier expressing the feeling of the signatoriva that the Vieeroyalty of Ireland was a mark of separation rather than of onion, and urging Her Majesty's Government to take into consideration the advisability of abolishing the office altogether. Lord Salisbury -replied that though it was obvious, front the announcement he had been enabled to make, that the Hovernment was not of the same opinion as the meal- I orialists, yet he would take the memorial into his most careful constieration, and would not allow himself to forget this moot important manifestation of lrish opinion.

div.p: BURYLEY GAZETTE, Febrrary 23rd. IIE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford load, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to encounter them in other mining sufferer in consequence. He first I I commenced with pains in his _ _ _ .
